newsitem.title: USA: For Clinton, celebration soon turns to reality.
newsitem.headline: For Clinton, celebration soon turns to reality.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, who began his second term with a call for reconciliation and then waltzed into the night at inaugural balls, now turns to the sobering task of governing.

Tens of thousands ignored the January cold to witness the inauguration on Monday of the 50-year-old Clinton, a Democrat who a mere two years ago was considered politically dead in the wake of the Republican congressional election landslide.

Instead of witnessing Clinton's departure from the political landscape as his four-year term expired, House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich and his fellow Republicans listened as their political foe spoke of cooperation and the need to avoid petty bickering.
Clinton's day of triumph began with a church service and ended in the early morning hours after visits to a record number of inaugural balls -- a total of 15 in all.
The president and his wife, Hillary, greeted by deliriously happy supporters at every party they visited, danced their way through a string of elegant inaugural celebrations.
"I just love him," enthused Edith Henig, of North Miami Beach, who came to Washington to catch a glimpse of the president at the Florida inaugural ball, the sixth on their list.
Clinton, who was beaming broadly for most of the evening, told a group of veterans at the first ball that being inaugurated was "better the second time around."
The first couple swayed to a range of music from the Isley Brothers to the Cuban-American rhythms of a brass band.

Together with daughter Chelsea, the Clintons earlier led a colorful parade down Pennsylvania Avenue that included floats, marching bands, baton twirlers, horses, clowns and costumed merrymakers from all 50 states.
On Tuesday, however, the magical moments were to give way to the reality of life in the White House.

Clinton had two items on the agenda of the first full day of his second term -- a meeting with economic advisers and the installation of new Democratic leaders to repair his party's image, which was badly tarnished by controversial 1996 fundraising tactics.
A White House official said the economic meeting was to focus on strategy for negotiating with the Republican Congress on the budget that Clinton will unveil on Feb. 6.

The official, who asked not to be indentified, said fixing Medicare's long-term financing problems was the trickiest issue to be resolved but said Clinton was optimistic he and the Republicans eventually would forge a deal.

Later in the day, Clinton was to attend a meeting of the Democratic National Committee. The group was to ratify his choice of Colorado Gov. Roy Romer as general chairman and Boston businessman Steve Grossman to be national chairman.
The two men and Clinton must deal with an uproar over party fundraising practices, including the collection of contributions from foreign donors, which is illegal under federal law.

Clinton's inaugural address, delivered on the steps of the West Front of the Capitol, stressed his willingness to cooperate with the Republican Congress -- noting that voters in November made their decision.

"The American people returned to office a president of one party and a Congress of another," he said. "Surely they did not do this to advance the politics of petty bickering and extreme partisanship they plainly deplore."

"No, they call on us instead to be repairers of the breach and to move on with America's mission," he said. "America demands and deserves big things from us and nothing big ever came from being small."
For both Clinton and Gingrich, a cooling of heated political rhetoric would be welcome.

Clinton still faces a probe of his Whitewater land dealings in Arkansas, as well as an attempt by a former Arkansas state employee to sue him for alleged sexual harassment in 1991 when he was governor.
On Tuesday, the U.S. House of Representatives was set to vote on a proposal to reprimand Gingrich and fine him $300,000 for violating House rules, climaxing two years of bitter partisan squabbling.
